_: Meta economy. Starting values, not tuned values — see docs/04-economy.md for the invariants these must satisfy and how to verify them with the simulation.
_anchor: A floor-level GREEDY SIM (no meta, no powers) clears 5 stages for 1,118 points in ~124 placements. That sim is NOT the floor: it evaluates every rotation in every position, and a first-time human clears 2 stages. Every number here used to be priced against the sim, which is why a real first run returned 35 spools against a 100-spool first unlock. See docs/04 §7.
_rule1: Payout keys off STAGES, never score. Score inflates when the player buys value upgrades; stages do not, because the target curve defines them. Keying payout to score creates a buy-more-earn-more spiral that destroys the curve (docs/04 §1).

payout._formula: spools = sum over s in 1..stagesReached of (base + perStage * s)
payout._payForStageReached: A run is paid for every stage it REACHED, not only the stages it cleared. The stage you fought and lost is a stage you played. This keeps rule 1 intact — a stage reached is still a stage, not a score — while removing the cliff where a run that died on stage 1 paid literally nothing.
payout._examples: died on stage 1 = 15 · cleared 2 = 60 · cleared 5 = 165 · cleared 8 = 315 · won = 510

shapeCosts._: Tier 1's five are free at install. 17 motifs to unlock, 13,680 spools total. dot alone is tier 4, at 3,600 - the single most expensive purchase in the game.
shapeCosts._inverted: Re-weighted 2026-11-11, the other half of the roster inversion in lib/core/shapes.dart. Pricing used to run size-ascending, so the small liquid motifs were free and the big blocks cost 12,700 of 13,730 spools - and at 100% unlocks the loadout was entirely tiers 1-2, so almost the whole shape economy bought pieces nobody fields. Now the big blocks are cheap and the two PRECISION motifs (i2, dot) are the most expensive purchases in the game. Total content is unchanged; what it buys is not.
shapeCosts._perSlot: A tier's prices are per PURCHASE SLOT, not per motif: costOfNthShapeInTier indexes by how many of that tier you already own. That is why dot and i2 need a tier of their own - inside a shared tier a player would simply buy them first at the cheapest slot price.

upgrades._: 15,400 spools. Rebuilt 2026-11-12: these used to be seven small flat numbers (+1 value, +2 moves, one shield) and they are now STRUCTURAL - slots, charges, guarantees, allowance - because the shop's job under docs/08 B7 is to sell a player out of jams, and a flat +1 cannot do that.
upgrades._wording: Added 2026-11-13 (UX review §7). Player-facing strings here say what the player GETS, in the words the rest of the game uses: a block is the piece, a cell is a square of the board. 'value' was never defined anywhere in the game, and with no yarn upgrade a placement scores nothing at all — so '+3 value' read as a small bonus on top of something, when it is in fact the whole of a placement's income. And a shield the player cannot price ('hold 3 shields') is 1,300 coins they will not spend.
upgrades._onAxis: Every one of these reduces jam risk or buys the tempo to play around a bad board. That is deliberate: a first run dies to a jam 58% of the time, so what the player wants is liquidity, slots and escape valves. Score upgrades (the yarns) are still here and still matter, but they are no longer the whole shop.

loadoutSlot9.effect: pick 9 blocks for your set instead of 8

loadoutSlot10.effect: pick 10 blocks for your set instead of 9

handful.effect: every refill includes a block of 3 cells or fewer

openingRhythm.effect: every level starts at x2.0 combo or better

startingSelvage.effect: 3 shields every level. A shield takes a combo break for you

fineYarn.effect: +3 points per cell for 1–2 cell blocks

standardYarn.effect: +3 points per cell for 3–4 cell blocks

heavyYarn.effect: +3 points per cell for 5+ cell blocks

_fourthSlotIsForSale: docs/04 3 refused to sell a 4th tray slot: 'the single largest power swing in the game', it 'alters the refill-on-empty rule the whole difficulty rests on', it 'roughly halves jam risk'. Every one of those is true and all three are now REASONS TO SELL IT. Under docs/08 B7 halving jam risk is precisely what the shop is for, and the refill-on-empty rule is the difficulty the player is buying their way out of. Second Shuttle stays in the draft and stacks on top, so a drafted 5th slot is still a real pick.
_invariant: The shop sells LIQUIDITY, and its job is measured on the jam rate: a 0%-unlock run dies to a jam about 58% of the time, buying i2 takes that to 20%, i3 and i4 to 7%, and a full account to 0%. That decline IS the progression curve and it is something a player can feel. The +4-stages-of-median-depth budget this field used to carry is GONE (docs/04 rule 2): never met, never visible from inside the game, and in arithmetic conflict with the three gates - if 100% unlocks must win reliably at median 12 and 0% must die around 6-7, the lift is +5 to +6 by definition. Three gates, all holding as of 2026-11-12: 0% jam-led and unwinnable, 85% winnable with a good run (19%), 100% reliable (63%). And note which lever got the last one: starter cards are the floor, targetGrowth moves everything at once, and an UPGRADE is the only thing a 0%-unlock account does not have - so making purchases strong raises the ceiling and leaves the floor alone.
